message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This bid is unusual in that it is not based on assumptions about demand: we tested the exact opening pattern at Ashgrove before asking for a penny, and measured the results hour by hour. The pilot showed strong uptake, with evening visits running close to daytime levels and Sunday sessions very popular with families, and new memberships up by about two-thirds on the year before. That gives Members real local evidence that the hours will be used. The costing is equally careful. Staffing is built up from first principles, hours times staff times weeks times branches at the correct graded rate with on-costs, and utilities are taken from actual pilot spend rather than estimates, all of which sums to £174,000. We also looked seriously at the cheaper self-service alternative and explain why it would cost more once building works are included. I am confident this is a well-tested, carefully costed proposal that delivers on the Council Plan.
</author>

<document>
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.
</document>
response:
# Review: Budget Justification, Extended Opening Hours (Westmoor Borough Council)

The structure is sound. The bid uses a pilot of the exact proposed pattern and builds staffing costs from first principles. However, the bid has an arithmetic error in its total and misreads its own pilot data on evening demand. It also misstates the pilot's length, and it overstates the value-for-money case.

## 1. The costs total £164,000, not £174,000

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| Staffing | £124,000 |
| Utilities and caretaking | £32,500 |
| Kiosk maintenance | £7,500 |
| **Correct sum** | **£164,000** |

The individual lines are calculated correctly: 10 × 2 × 50 × 5 = 5,000 hours × £24.80 = £124,000, and £6,500 × 5 = £32,500. Only the total is wrong. Either a £10,000 item is missing from the table, or the bid is £10,000 higher than its own costing. This needs fixing before Members see it, because it undermines the "carefully costed" claim.

## 2. Evening use was less than half of daytime levels

The bid says evening visits "averaged close to the weekday daytime level." Table 1 shows otherwise:

| Slot | Visits per hour | Evening as % of slot |
|---|---|---|
| Weekday 9–12 | 46 | 46% |
| Weekday 12–5 | 58 | 36% |
| **Tue/Thu 5–8 pm (new)** | **21** | — |
| Sunday 11–3 (new) | 52 | — |

Evening use ran at roughly **36–46% of daytime**. **Sunday** is the slot that came close to daytime levels. The evening slots still have a good story: the fully booked job club directly serves the working-age and job-seeking aims in the Council Plan. But the bid should argue from that, not from a comparison the data don't support.

The pilot also says nothing about any other branch, so it can't show that hours "will be well used across all five branches." Section 7 itself concedes that Ashgrove is the busiest branch.

## 3. The pilot ran for six months, not twelve

Section 3 gives the dates as October 2025 to March 2026, which is six months. The conclusion calls it a "twelve-month Ashgrove pilot." The pilot length also affects two other parts of the bid:

- **Utilities were scaled up from a winter-only period.** Heating and lighting for dark evenings between October and March will exceed the full-year average, so the £6,500 per branch may be overstated. That works in the Council's favour, but it should be explained.
- **The pilot captures no seasonal variation in visits.** Summer evening and Sunday demand may differ from winter demand.

## 4. Current hours don't add up to 38

Table 1 shows weekday opening from 9 am to 5 pm (8 hours × 5 days = 40 hours) plus Saturday from 9 am to 1 pm (4 hours), which totals **44 hours**. The bid says the branches currently open for 38 hours. Perhaps the branches close for a half-day or a lunch break, or not every branch keeps Ashgrove's pattern. Either way, the "38 to 48 hours" claim needs reconciling with the table.

## 5. The value-for-money comparison is generous

The 84,000 figure checks out arithmetically. Each branch would add 6 hours × 21 visits plus 4 hours × 52 visits = 334 visits a week. Over 50 weeks that's 16,700 visits per branch, or 83,500 across five branches. But there are three problems:

- **It assumes all five branches match Ashgrove,** which the risks section acknowledges is the busiest branch. If the other four achieve half of Ashgrove's rates, additional visits fall to about 50,000. The cost per visit then rises to about £3.30–£3.50, roughly equal to the borough average rather than well below it.
- **It counts gross visits, not net.** Some Sunday and evening visitors may simply have moved from Saturday or daytime visits. The bid doesn't say whether daytime visits at Ashgrove changed during the pilot, and that data should be available.
- **The comparison isn't like for like.** The marginal cost of extra hours (about £2) is set against an average cost per visit (£3.40) that includes fixed building and management overheads. Marginal cost is naturally lower.

The new-membership figure is accurate: 1,140 against 690 is a 65% rise, which is about two-thirds. However, the bid doesn't show how many of those people joined during the new hours. Without that, it can't attribute the rise to the extended opening.

## 6. The self-service alternative is only more expensive in the short term

The author's summary says self-service "would cost more once building works are included." The document itself doesn't make that claim, and the numbers only partly support it:

- Cutting staffing by two-thirds saves about £83,000 a year.
- Building works cost about £60,000 × 5 = **£300,000, as a one-off capital cost**.
- So the works pay for themselves in about **3.6 years**, and self-service is cheaper over any longer period.

The stronger argument, which the bid already makes, concerns the service itself. Unstaffed hours can't run the job club or family sessions. The bid should lead with that point, present the cost comparison honestly over a multi-year period, and note that capital and revenue funding come from different budgets.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Kiosk maintenance (£7,500).** It isn't explained why a staffed option needs kiosk upgrades. If they would be needed anyway, they don't belong in this bid.
- **Staffing rate.** The £24.80 rate "includes an enhancement for Sunday working." The bid should say whether this is a blended rate across all 10 hours or whether Sunday is costed separately. Applying the Sunday premium to the evening hours would overstate the cost.
- **Recruitment.** Relying on existing part-time staff worked at one branch, but it's worth confirming there is enough interest across all five.

## What holds up

- The staffing method (hours × staff × weeks × branches with on-costs) is clear, and its arithmetic is correct.
- Testing the exact proposed pattern first is genuinely good practice, and Sunday demand is strong.
- The rationale is well tied to the survey (44% of non-users aged 25–54) and to the Council Plan.
- The six-month usage review is a sensible safeguard.

## Suggested changes before submission

1. Correct the total to £164,000, or add and explain the missing £10,000.
2. Describe evening use accurately (about 40% of daytime) and make the case through the job club and working-age access.
3. Correct "twelve-month" to six months, and note the winter timing of the pilot.
4. Reconcile the current 38 hours with the opening pattern in Table 1.
5. Show a lower-demand scenario for the other four branches, and state whether pilot daytime visits fell.
6. Present the self-service comparison over several years, separating capital from revenue, and lead with the argument about the service.
7. Explain or remove the kiosk line, and clarify how the Sunday enhancement is applied.

The proposal may well be worth funding, and Sunday opening in particular looks well evidenced. But as written, the total doesn't match its components, and the evening-demand and pilot-length claims contradict the bid's own data. Those errors would be easy for a Member or finance officer to spot.
